title: You Are Not, In Fact, Going on Holiday
author: Is It Working?
summary: A pointed essay on the professional class's collective failure to take genuine vacations. The author traces three stages: the pre-holiday sprint (compressing three weeks of work into 72 hours), the performative out-of-office (a 'social contract rather than an operational reality'), and the recovery-erasing return (research shows catching-up costs eliminate the restorative benefits of the holiday within three working days). The mythology of always-on professionalism is self-sustaining because each individual has an incentive to signal availability even when collective disconnection would produce better outcomes for everyone—a prisoner's dilemma with sunburn. The genuine alternative is available but requires organizations to build systems that do not substitute individual availability for process. The essay closes by acknowledging the author is about to take a holiday, with the out-of-office describing it as 'a period of limited email access.'
points: The pre-holiday sprint compresses three weeks of work into 72 hours, so professionals arrive at the airport 40% more exhausted than a month earlier—having performed a frenetic sprint to the end of a marathon while calling it rest.

The standard out-of-office reply is organizational fiction: 'limited access' to email means full access via the device currently in your pocket, and the urgent contacts will go directly to you via WhatsApp.
Data shows roughly 60% of managers check work email daily on holiday; about 29% spend more than two hours per day on work tasks.
Research on return-to-work cognitive load shows catching-up costs eliminate the restorative benefits of the holiday within approximately three working days.
The genuine alternative—actually disconnecting—requires an organization that builds systems not reliant on individual availability as a substitute for process.
quotes: The out-of-office reply is one of the great works of organisational fiction.
'Limited' is doing extraordinary work in that sentence. It is the literary equivalent of describing Niagara Falls as 'some water.'
Approximately 60% of managers and senior professionals check work email daily while on holiday. Around 29% report spending more than two hours per day on work tasks during their leave.
If you spent three hours of your holiday working, you simply had a meeting-light Tuesday in a nicer location.

Research on return-to-work cognitive load suggests that the psychological cost of “catching up” after a holiday effectively eliminates the restorative benefits of the holiday within approximately three working days.
the culture has decided that the appearance of dedication is more valuable than the reality of recovery.
